description: Current scientific understanding of how reading and hearing connect in the human brain. The substrate uses this vocabulary to reason about whether its own reading faculty should be literally connected to its hearing/phonology stack (sharing the same circuitry / pipeline) or figuratively connected (using analogous concepts at the level of comprehension). The decision is for the agent — this Mt provides the facts it reasons over.
wiring_note: Reading is an integrated faculty — it routes through BOTH the phonology stack (prosody + speech_science: abstract-phonology + subvocalization + auditory cortex circuitry, even without acoustic input) AND the comprehension stack (narrative_convention + pragmatics + reference + figurative: the substrate's existing comprehension scaffold the agent reads ANY speech or narrative against). Wiring this BEFORE speech understanding is forward-solved is the position the user named: 'wire the feeling' — the architecture commits to integration; the components catch up. Hearing-side and comprehension-side both wired so that reading is what the entity does, not a parsing pipeline.

concepts.name: visual_word_form_area
concepts.definition: VWFA — region of left ventral occipitotemporal cortex specialized for recognizing written words. Despite being in 'visual' cortex, it responds to BOTH written and spoken language. 2025 fMRI + sEEG evidence: distinct neural populations within VWFA encode written vs spoken language, but they SHARE the same cortical region. Cross-modal by design.
concepts.cites_prior_work: Imaging Neuroscience 2025 (MIT Press); Dehaene et al. on VWFA

concepts.name: grapheme_to_phoneme_conversion
concepts.definition: The brain process by which written letters are converted into corresponding speech sounds. The substrate of the non-lexical (phonological) reading route. Lets readers pronounce unfamiliar words. Subvocalization is the engine that drives this conversion in silent reading.
concepts.cites_prior_work: Coltheart dual-route model; phonological reading neuroscience

concepts.name: lexical_route_reading
concepts.definition: Direct visual-to-meaning pathway. Frequent / familiar words are recognized as whole units; their meaning is accessed without going through phonology. Connectionist evidence: dorsal extrastriate cortex links directly to parietal+frontal phonological nodes for frequent regular words.

concepts.name: non_lexical_route_reading
concepts.definition: Phonological / sublexical pathway. Unfamiliar words, pseudowords, and slow careful reading go through grapheme-to-phoneme conversion. A POSTERIOR VENTRAL pathway. Both routes operate in parallel; reading uses whichever delivers meaning first per item.

concepts.name: dual_route_reading_model
concepts.definition: Coltheart's model: reading uses two routes in parallel. Lexical (direct visual recognition) for familiar words; non-lexical (phonological decoding) for unfamiliar ones. Both routes work simultaneously; competition between them produces the reading time differences observed for word frequency / regularity.

concepts.name: subvocalization
concepts.definition: The inner-speech rehearsal that occurs during silent reading. fMRI: Broca's area, Wernicke's area, AND auditory cortex active during silent reading even with no sound. Critical for comprehension — suppressing subvocalization drops comprehension 25-50%. Drives grapheme-to-phoneme conversion.
concepts.cites_prior_work: fMRI studies of silent reading; Baddeley working memory

concepts.name: phonological_loop
concepts.definition: Baddeley's working-memory component for verbal information. Two parts: phonological store (the 'inner ear' — holds speech sounds in temporal order) and articulatory rehearsal loop (the 'inner voice' — re-activates / refreshes the store). Critical for reading because it holds early segments of a sentence while later segments are processed.

concepts.name: phonological_store_inner_ear
concepts.definition: Sub-component of the phonological loop. Holds verbal information in a sound-based format for up to ~2 seconds before it decays. Articulatory rehearsal can refresh it.

concepts.name: articulatory_rehearsal_inner_voice
concepts.definition: Sub-component of the phonological loop. The 'inner voice' that re-reads / re-says the contents of the phonological store, preventing decay. This IS subvocalization. Active during silent reading.

concepts.name: auditory_word_form
concepts.definition: Cortical representation that combines acoustic-phonetic features, prosodic elements, and lexical information. Sub-lexical phonological content in the superior temporal gyrus is transformed into word-level representations by higher-order brain regions. The 'hearing equivalent' of the visual word form.
concepts.cites_prior_work: Neuron 2025 (Cell Press) on auditory word form encoding

concepts.name: abstract_phonology
concepts.definition: Phonological representations that are MODALITY-INDEPENDENT — they encode speech-sound structure without being tied to either acoustic input or motor output. 2025 PNAS finding: reading ability in BOTH deaf and hearing adults is linked to neural representations of abstract phonology derived from visual speech. Phonology is not just sound — it's structure.
concepts.cites_prior_work: PNAS 2025 on deaf and hearing readers

concepts.name: phonology_deafness_evidence
concepts.definition: Deaf readers also use phonological representations to read — but theirs are derived from visual speech (lip reading) and orthographic patterns, not from acoustic experience. This shows phonology is NOT inherently auditory; it's an abstract structural layer that reading recruits regardless of the input modality used to learn it.

concepts.name: cross_modal_letter_speech_sound_integration
concepts.definition: The brain process by which a visual letter is bound to its associated speech sound. Develops during reading acquisition; deficient integration is a marker of dyslexia. The binding involves auditory cortex AND visual cortex AND inferior frontal regions.

concepts.name: phonological_deficit_dyslexia
concepts.definition: Dominant theory of developmental dyslexia: the core deficit is in phonological processing — representing, storing, retrieving speech sounds. Dyslexic readers have intact visual processing but impaired phonological access from print. Strongest evidence FOR the phonological route being load-bearing in reading.

concepts.name: literal_connection_interpretation
concepts.definition: Architectural reading where the substrate's reading faculty SHARES CIRCUITRY with its hearing faculty — text input flows through the substrate's phonology / cochlear / auditory cortex stack before reaching higher-level comprehension. Mirrors the human VWFA's cross-modal encoding + subvocalization circuit.

concepts.name: figurative_connection_interpretation
concepts.definition: Architectural reading where the substrate's reading and hearing faculties use ANALOGOUS BUT SEPARATE concepts. Both pipelines arrive at the same comprehension surface (narrative_convention, trope_play, pragmatics) but text doesn't literally go through phonology / cochlea. The shared structure is at the abstract-phonology + comprehension level.

concepts.name: modality_invariant_phonology_argument
concepts.definition: Argument from the deaf-reader evidence: phonology is modality-invariant; it's an abstract structural representation, not bound to acoustic input. If true, the substrate's reading faculty needs to share PHONOLOGY (abstract structure) with hearing, not literal cochlear processing. Supports the figurative interpretation.

concepts.name: shared_circuitry_argument
concepts.definition: Argument from the VWFA cross-modal evidence: even visual cortex regions specialized for reading respond to spoken language. The brain reuses the same cortical area for both input modes. Supports the literal interpretation — the substrate would share circuitry between reading and hearing, not just concepts.

concepts.name: subvocalization_load_bearing_argument
concepts.definition: Argument from the subvocalization evidence: silent reading DOES recruit auditory cortex; comprehension drops 25-50% when subvocalization is suppressed. The phonological route is not optional — it's load-bearing for comprehension. Supports the literal interpretation.

rules.name: reading_recruits_phonology_in_humans
then: Broca's area, Wernicke's area, and auditory cortex all activate
subvocalization (inner voice) drives grapheme-to-phoneme conversion
comprehension drops 25-50% if subvocalization is suppressed
rules.why: Empirical evidence from fMRI of silent reading. The phonological route is load-bearing, not optional.
rules.cites_prior_work: Multiple fMRI studies; phonological loop research

rules.name: phonology_is_modality_invariant_in_reading
if: a person reads (whether hearing or deaf)
then: their reading ability correlates with neural representations of ABSTRACT phonology
for deaf readers, the phonology is derived from visual speech (lip reading) + orthography
phonology in reading is structural, not acoustic
rules.why: PNAS 2025: deaf readers' reading ability tracks abstract phonological representations. Shows phonology is a structural layer, not an audio-input layer.

rules.name: VWFA_encodes_both_written_and_spoken_language
if: a region of left ventral occipitotemporal cortex is specialized for reading (VWFA)
then: it ALSO responds to spoken language
distinct neural populations within it encode written vs spoken language
the cross-modal response is via shared circuit, not just shared concept
rules.why: 2025 fMRI + sEEG evidence (Imaging Neuroscience): the brain reuses the same cortical area for both modalities.

rules.name: dual_route_means_two_pathways_in_parallel
then: a lexical (direct visual-to-meaning) pathway operates in parallel with
a non-lexical (phonological grapheme-to-phoneme) pathway
frequent regular words use the lexical route preferentially; unfamiliar words use the non-lexical route
rules.why: Coltheart's dual-route model + connectivity neuroimaging evidence.

rules.name: literal_connection_requires_subvocalization_circuit
if: the substrate's reading faculty literally shares circuitry with its hearing faculty
AND the substrate has a phonology stack (cochlear_nucleus, auditory_cortex, prosody)
then: text input flows through grapheme-to-phoneme conversion first
the substrate's phonological_loop equivalent rehearses subvocalized content
comprehension recruits the auditory_cortex-equivalent
the cost is shared with what the audio pipeline already pays
rules.why: Mirrors the human VWFA+subvocalization circuit. Maps directly onto existing substrate audio infrastructure.

rules.name: figurative_connection_requires_shared_phonology_concepts_only
if: the substrate's reading and hearing faculties are analogous but separate
then: both pipelines arrive at the same comprehension surface (narrative, trope, pragmatics)
abstract_phonology concepts (structural, not acoustic) are shared
but text doesn't literally go through the cochlea / auditory_cortex
rules.why: Mirrors the modality-invariant phonology evidence (deaf readers). Phonology as structure, not sound.

rules.name: the_choice_is_determined_by_substrate_priors
if: the substrate has rich existing audio / phonology / cochlear infrastructure
AND the substrate's vocabulary covers abstract phonology AND acoustic phonology
then: the literal interpretation is cheap to enact (shared circuitry already exists)
the figurative interpretation requires duplicating phonological structure as a separate abstract layer
the literal interpretation is the more parsimonious choice given the substrate's current state
rules.why: Parsimony argument: the substrate already has the audio infrastructure; reusing it for reading mirrors how humans do it and avoids duplication.
